scores.reason: A random C-peptide with concurrent glucose, in an insulin-treated person more than 3 years from diagnosis, determines classification and so whether insulin can be replaced or genetics sent. Autoantibodies are the primary test at diagnosis, so it is not a required step.
sources: PMID 34590174 DOI 10.1007/s00125-021-05568-3 full text (via usecases-verified.md row 6, skeptic-verified)

scores.reason: A random C-peptide is a routine laboratory test with no timed protocol that a primary care physician can order in a stable insulin-treated patient with doubtful type. Interpretation rules (greater than 3 years, renal function, glucose above 4 mmol/L) and thresholds that differ between sources need care, and many unclear cases go to an endocrinologist.

One blood draw, no fasting and no provocation, so burden is low. A false-low value (renal impairment, low glucose, early after diagnosis) could wrongly label someone insulin-deficient. A false-high value could lead to insulin withdrawal in a person with T1D, so the result must be read against the caveats.
sources: PMID 34590174 DOI 10.1007/s00125-021-05568-3 full text (via row 6 caveats)

scores.reason: Misclassifying insulin-requiring diabetes as T2D and withdrawing insulin risks ketoacidosis and hospitalisation. Missing a MODY or insulin-independent T2D mostly costs unnecessary injections, so the typical harm is serious but not usually fatal.
sources: PMID 34590174 DOI 10.1007/s00125-021-05568-3 full text (via row 6; the 11% reclassified figure)

scores.reason: Insulin and glucose at the nadir support the diagnosis of postprandial hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia and help exclude insulinoma, drugs and exogenous insulin. Management (diet, acarbose, specialist referral) would start from documented low glucose with symptoms alone, and no accepted insulin threshold exists.

A reliable result needs insulin and glucose drawn at the symptomatic nadir or during a supervised mixed-meal test. That is a specialist protocol, and in primary care a spontaneous sample is rarely captured. Patients are usually referred to endocrinology.

A mixed-meal test deliberately provokes symptomatic hypoglycaemia in patients who may have neuroglycopenia and unawareness, so supervision is needed. Without an accepted threshold a false-positive or false-negative insulin value can mislead, but it rarely triggers harmful treatment.

Undiagnosed post-bariatric hypoglycaemia causes seizures, loss of consciousness, falls, road accidents and unawareness. Missing an insulinoma or exogenous insulin adds to that. Insulin is only one part of getting the right decision, so confidence is low.

A HOMA-IR above 3.0 (fasting insulin with glucose) would choose among accepted options: pioglitazone for secondary stroke prevention in prediabetes. Both guidelines say considered and neither names an assay or threshold. IRIS never tested whether a lower HOMA-IR means no benefit, and a clinician can treat on stroke plus prediabetes alone.
sources: PMID 26886418 DOI 10.1056/nejmoa1506930 abstract (HOMA-IR above 3.0 entry criterion) and full text via PMC4887756 (via row 13)
ADA Standards of Care 2026 section 3, Rec 3.13 (via row 13 skeptic reading)

scores.reason: Patients are seen by neurology, post-stroke clinics or primary care, and the measure is a fasting insulin plus glucose with a calculation, which is not a routine panel. The fasting draw is practical but the assay is not standardised, IRIS used a central laboratory, and the result is rarely requested in practice.
sources: PMID 26886418 DOI 10.1056/nejmoa1506930 full text via PMC4887756 (via row 13: central laboratories because insulin not standardised)

scores.reason: The draw is low burden, but the result gates a drug with real harm (weight gain over 4.5 kg in 52% of the pioglitazone arm, oedema, fracture, heart failure risk). A false-positive value from an unstandardised assay exposes a patient to those effects. A false-negative withholds a drug with a 24% relative risk reduction.

The outcome at stake is recurrent stroke or myocardial infarction (9.0% against 11.8% over 4.8 years in IRIS), which means permanent disability or death. Not having HOMA-IR would not usually prevent treatment, so confidence in this stakes score for the measurement itself is low.

anchor_issues: Row 6 D1: determines classification (3) versus required step (4). Chose 3 because autoantibodies are the primary test at diagnosis and C-peptide is second line.
Row 5 D1: the diagnosis is supported by insulin plus glucose, but treatment starts without it. Chose 2 (supports a diagnosis) rather than 3.

Row 13 D1: IRIS used the measure as entry criterion, which could be read as eligibility criterion (4), but anchor 12 limits 4 to legal or regulatory requirements and guidelines do not require the measurement. Chose 2.
Row 13 D5: no anchor for a fasting test that is routine to draw but not a standard panel and not standardised. Chose 2.
D6 anchors mix patient burden and false-result consequences; where the two differ (rows 6 and 13) I scored the worse of the two within one point of the burden score.

S is defined as the consequence of not having the information, but for rows 5 and 13 other information (glucose, clinical picture) covers most of the decision. I scored the harm of the wrong decision in that situation and marked confidence low.
assumptions: Row 6 scored for random C-peptide in insulin-treated adults with uncertain type (the Holt 2021 situation), not for diabetes classification at diagnosis.
Row 5 scored for insulin at symptomatic nadir or mixed-meal test (mixed-meal / post-load measure type); fasting measures were not used.
Row 13 scored for fasting-based HOMA-IR (fasting insulin and glucose), the IRIS measure.
